title: Why Your Bank Pays You 0.01% (And Where the Rest Goes)
alts: Savings Account Interest Explained: Why Banks Pay You Almost Nothing
Your Bank Earns 3.9% On Your Money. You Get 0.01%.
line1: Why does your savings account pay almost nothing? Dave's $5,000 earned 50 cents, while his bank could earn 3.9% on it at the Fed.
summary: Dave's $5,000 savings account paid him fifty cents last year, so he follows his cash into the bank to see where the rest goes. We explain the net interest margin with a lemonade stand (3.32% in the FDIC's Q2 2026 Quarterly Banking Profile), the three jobs your deposits do (loans, Treasury bills and interest on reserves at the Federal Reserve), how big banks earn around $1 billion a day, and why sticky money lets them pay savers so little. Then we compare high-yield savings accounts, CDs, money market funds and T-bills, explain the $250,000 FDIC insurance limit, and show how inflation eats low-interest savings.
